entries.1:1: This starts a family list with Adam and the first generations after him. It reminds the reader that the story of God's people begins with real people from the very beginning.
entries.1:2: The list continues with more early ancestors in Adam's family line. It shows the reader that these names were passed down as part of a real family history.
entries.1:3: More names follow in the same family line, including Enoch and Methuselah. It tells the reader that God's story moves forward through ordinary generations of people.
entries.1:4: Noah's three sons are named here, the families from whom the nations came. It shows the reader that all peoples trace back to one family.
entries.1:5: This lists the sons of Japheth, one of Noah's sons. It shows the reader how the nations spread out from Noah's family.
entries.1:6: These are the grandsons of Japheth through his son Gomer. It keeps showing how different peoples came from one family tree.
entries.1:7: This names the sons of Javan, another line from Japheth. It reminds the reader that many nations have a shared origin.
entries.1:8: This lists the sons of Ham, another of Noah's sons. It shows the reader that the nations of the world came from Noah's three sons.
entries.1:9: These are Ham's grandchildren through Cush and Raamah. It continues tracing how different peoples and regions came to be.
entries.1:10: Nimrod is singled out as the first great man on earth. It shows the reader that even famous, powerful people fit into God's larger story.
entries.1:11: This lists peoples that came from Egypt, one of Ham's sons. It shows the reader that whole nations grew from these early families.
entries.1:12: The list continues with more peoples from Egypt, including the Philistines. It reminds the reader that Israel's neighbors also had a place in this family history.
entries.1:13: This names Canaan's sons, starting with his oldest, Zidon. It shows the reader where the peoples of Canaan came from.
entries.1:14: These are more peoples descended from Canaan. It shows the reader that the land Israel would later enter was already filled with related nations.
entries.1:15: The list of Canaanite peoples continues. It reminds the reader that these groups were all part of one extended family.
entries.1:16: This finishes the list of Canaan's descendants. It shows the reader that the whole region's peoples trace back to Noah's family.
entries.1:17: This lists the sons of Shem, the line that leads to Abraham. It shows the reader where God's chosen people came from.
entries.1:18: The line continues from Arpachshad down to Eber. It shows the reader that the family line was carefully remembered through the generations.
entries.1:19: Eber's son Peleg was named for a division of the earth in his time. It shows the reader that big events in history were remembered through family names.
entries.1:20: This lists the sons of Joktan, another line from Eber. It shows the reader how the family spread into many branches.
entries.1:21: More sons of Joktan are named here. It keeps showing the reader how one family grew into many peoples.
entries.1:22: The list of Joktan's sons continues. It reminds the reader that these names stood for real families and tribes.
entries.1:23: This ends the list of Joktan's sons. It shows the reader that this whole branch of the family is accounted for.
entries.1:24: The focus now narrows to the line from Shem down to Abraham. It shows the reader that God's plan moves through a specific family line.
entries.1:25: The family line continues through Eber, Peleg, and Reu. It reminds the reader that each generation mattered in God's story.
entries.1:26: More ancestors are named on the way to Abraham. It shows the reader that Abraham came from a long line of real people.
entries.1:27: The line reaches Abram, who is also called Abraham. It shows the reader that this is the man God would later make great promises to.
entries.1:28: Abraham's two sons, Isaac and Ishmael, are named. It shows the reader that both branches of Abraham's family are remembered.
entries.1:29: This lists Ishmael's sons, starting with his oldest. It shows the reader that Ishmael's family also became many peoples.
entries.1:30: More of Ishmael's sons are named. It reminds the reader that God's care extended to Abraham's other descendants too.
entries.1:31: This finishes the list of Ishmael's sons. It shows the reader that Ishmael's family line was fully recorded.
entries.1:32: This lists the sons Abraham had with Keturah. It shows the reader that Abraham's family spread widely beyond Isaac and Ishmael.
entries.1:33: These are the sons of Midian, one of Keturah's sons. It reminds the reader that many peoples came from Abraham's household.
entries.1:34: The line now focuses on Isaac's twin sons, Esau and Israel. It shows the reader that the story is narrowing toward the nation of Israel.
entries.1:35: This lists the sons of Esau, also called Edom. It shows the reader that Esau's family became its own people group.
entries.1:36: These are Esau's grandsons through Eliphaz, including Amalek. It shows the reader how Esau's family grew into clans and peoples.
entries.1:37: This names the sons of Reuel, another of Esau's sons. It continues showing how Esau's descendants spread out.
entries.1:38: This lists the sons of Seir, the people already living in the region of Edom. It shows the reader that Esau's family mixed with existing local peoples.
entries.1:39: These are Lotan's children, including his sister Timna. It reminds the reader that the record includes whole families, not just the men.
entries.1:40: This lists more descendants of Seir's sons. It shows the reader that the peoples of Edom had a detailed, remembered family history.
entries.1:41: This is a family list naming the descendants of Anah through his son Dishon. It reminds the reader that ordinary families and their names mattered to God and were carefully remembered.
entries.1:42: Another short list of descendants from Ezer and Dishan. These names show that the writer is tracing real family lines, and it encourages us to value the people in our own family history.
entries.1:43: This begins a list of kings who ruled in Edom before Israel had a king. It shows that God was at work in other nations too, and that history moves forward under his timing.
entries.1:44: When King Bela died, Jobab took his place as king. It is a simple reminder that leaders come and go, and life continues after them.
entries.1:45: After Jobab died, Husham from the land of Teman became king. The list keeps showing that each ruler had a turn and then was replaced.
entries.1:46: Hadad became king after Husham and won a battle against Midian in Moab. It shows that these early kings faced real conflicts and that God allowed them their victories.
entries.1:47: When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah became the next king. The pattern continues, showing that no human king rules forever.
entries.1:48: After Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth by the river took the throne. It is another step in the steady record of Edom's rulers.
entries.1:49: Baal-hanan became king when Shaul died. The list keeps its simple focus on who ruled next, reminding us that God keeps track of ordinary history.
entries.1:50: Hadad became king after Baal-hanan, and the writer also names his town and his wife's family. It shows that even personal details like marriage and hometown were worth remembering.
entries.1:51: Hadad's line ended, and Edom was then led by chiefs rather than kings. This marks a change in how the nation was governed and shows that systems of leadership change over time.
entries.1:52: This continues the list of Edom's chiefs, naming three more. It reminds the reader that many people shared leadership and each one is recorded.
entries.1:53: Three more chiefs of Edom are named here. The careful listing shows that God values each person, even those we know nothing else about.
entries.1:54: The list closes with the last chiefs and says these were the chiefs of Edom. It wraps up the record and reminds us that God remembers whole peoples and their leaders, not just Israel.
entries.2:1: This lists the twelve sons of Israel, the men whose families became the twelve tribes. It reminds the reader that the whole nation traces back to one family.
entries.2:2: This finishes the list of Israel's twelve sons. Each name stands for a tribe, so the reader sees the full family tree of the nation.
entries.2:3: Judah had three sons by a Canaanite woman, and his oldest son Er was so wicked that God ended his life. It shows that being born into the right family did not excuse doing evil.
entries.2:4: Judah's daughter-in-law Tamar gave him two more sons, Perez and Zerah, making five sons in all. It shows God's family line moving forward even through messy family situations.
entries.2:5: Perez had two sons, Hezron and Hamul. This keeps track of the family line that would become important in Israel's history.
entries.2:6: Zerah had five sons. The writer is simply recording the branches of Judah's family so later generations know where they came from.
entries.2:7: Achan, from this family line, brought trouble on Israel by taking things God had said were off-limits. It warns the reader that one person's disobedience can hurt many others.
entries.2:8: Ethan had a son named Azariah. This is another short link in the family record.
entries.2:9: Hezron had three sons: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai. The line through Ram will lead to King David.
entries.2:10: Ram's family line went through Amminadab to Nahshon, a leader of Judah's tribe. It shows God was building a line of leaders over many generations.
entries.2:11: The family line continued from Nahshon to Salma to Boaz. Boaz is the same man readers meet in the story of Ruth.
entries.2:12: Boaz was the father of Obed, and Obed was the father of Jesse. The line is getting closer to David.
entries.2:13: Jesse had several sons, starting with Eliab as the oldest. These brothers are the family David grew up in.
entries.2:14: This continues the list of Jesse's sons, naming the fourth and fifth. It shows David was not the only son in the family.
entries.2:15: Jesse's sixth son was Ozem, and the seventh was David. It highlights that David, the great king, was the youngest of many brothers.
entries.2:16: David had two sisters, Zeruiah and Abigail, and Zeruiah's three sons became famous warriors. It shows David's family included tough, capable men.
entries.2:17: Abigail's son was Amasa, whose father was an Ishmaelite. It shows the family was connected to people outside Israel as well.
entries.2:18: Caleb had children with his wife Azubah. The writer keeps tracing the branches of this large family.
entries.2:19: After Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, and she became the mother of Hur. Life went on, and the family line continued through a second wife.
entries.2:20: Hur was the father of Uri, and Uri was the father of Bezalel. Bezalel is the craftsman who later helped build the tabernacle.
entries.2:21: Hezron married a daughter of Machir when he was sixty and had a son named Segub. It shows God giving children even later in life.
entries.2:22: Segub's son Jair controlled twenty-three towns in Gilead. It shows this family gained real land and influence.
entries.2:23: Other groups captured sixty of those towns from Jair's family. It reminds the reader that land and power can be lost, not just gained.
entries.2:24: After Hezron died, his wife had a son named Asshur, who founded Tekoa. The family kept growing even after the father was gone.
entries.2:25: Jerahmeel, Hezron's oldest son, had five sons, with Ram the oldest. This begins a new branch of the family record.
entries.2:26: Jerahmeel had a second wife named Atarah, who had a son named Onam. It shows the family had more than one household.
entries.2:27: Ram, Jerahmeel's oldest son, had three sons. The record keeps naming each generation.
entries.2:28: Onam had two sons, and Shammai had two sons. This is another step in tracking the family line.
entries.2:29: Abishur's wife Abihail had two sons by him. The writer includes the wives' names too, showing they mattered in the family story.
entries.2:30: Nadab had two sons, but Seled died without having children. It shows some family lines came to an end.
entries.2:31: The line went from Appaim to Ishi to Sheshan to Ahlai. This keeps the record moving forward one generation at a time.
entries.2:32: Jada had two sons, and Jether died without children. Again, not every branch of the family continued.
entries.2:33: Jonathan had two sons, and this closes out the list of Jerahmeel's descendants. It marks the end of one section of the family record.
entries.2:34: Sheshan had only daughters and an Egyptian servant named Jarha. It sets up an unusual turn in the family story.
entries.2:35: Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to his servant Jarha, and they had a son named Attai. It shows God's family line continuing through a servant and a daughter, not just through sons.
entries.2:36: The line went from Attai to Nathan to Zabad. The family kept going through the generations.
entries.2:37: Zabad's son was Ephlal, and Ephlal's son was Obed. This is another link in the chain.
entries.2:38: Obed's son was Jehu, and Jehu's son was Azariah. The record continues steadily.
entries.2:39: Azariah's son was Helez, and Helez's son was Eleasah. Each name shows the family surviving and growing.
entries.2:40: Eleasah's son was Sismai, and Sismai's son was Shallum. The list keeps tracing the line faithfully.
entries.2:41: This verse simply lists a family line: Shallum was Jekamiah's father, and Jekamiah was Elishama's father. It reminds the reader that God keeps track of ordinary people across the generations, not just famous ones.
entries.2:42: Caleb's oldest son was Mareshah, and Mareshah's family line led to Ziph and Hebron. These names also became towns in Israel, showing how a family grew into a lasting place among God's people.
entries.2:43: This lists the four sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema. It is a record of a family branch, reminding the reader that each person in God's family history mattered.
entries.2:44: Shema's line went through Raham to Jorkeam, and Rekem was the father of Shammai. These brief family links show that God remembers people whose names we would otherwise never know.
entries.2:45: Shammai's son was Maon, and Maon's son was Beth-zur. Again these names became towns, showing how one family's story became part of the land God gave his people.
entries.2:46: Caleb's servant-wife Ephah had three sons, and one of them, Haran, became the father of Gazez. This shows that even family members with lower status were included in God's record of his people.
entries.2:47: This lists the six sons of Jahdai. It is a plain family record, reminding the reader that God values each ordinary person in the long story of his people.
entries.2:48: Caleb's servant-wife Maacah had two sons, Sheber and Tirhanah. The text quietly includes her and her children, showing that God's family record includes people we might overlook.
entries.2:49: Shaaph's line led to Madmannah, Sheva, Machbena, and Gibea, and Caleb's daughter Achsah is named here too. Women and men alike are part of this family story, and each name points to real people God cared for.
entries.2:50: This begins the family line of Hur, Ephrathah's oldest son, starting with Shobal, who was the father of Kiriath-jearim. It shows how one branch of the family became linked to a specific town.
entries.2:51: Salma was the father of Beth-lehem, and Hareph was the father of Beth-gader. These names connect families to towns, showing how God's people settled and grew in the land.
entries.2:52: Shobal, the father of Kiriath-jearim, had sons, including Haroeh and half of the Manahathites. This records how a family group split and spread out over time.
entries.2:53: This lists the family groups that came from Kiriath-jearim, including the Zorathites and Eshtaolites. It shows that whole communities grew from these family lines, and God kept track of them all.
entries.2:54: Salma's descendants included the people of Beth-lehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab, and part of the Manahathites and Zorites. This shows how one family's descendants became several recognizable groups in Israel.
entries.2:55: This names families of scribes living at Jabez who were Kenites descended from Hammath and linked to the Rechabites. It reminds the reader that people with practical jobs like copying records were also part of God's people and his story.
entries.3:1: This lists the first sons born to David while he ruled from Hebron, naming each son and his mother. It reminds the reader that David's family history was recorded in detail, with real people and real mothers behind each name.
entries.3:2: This continues the list of David's sons born in Hebron, including Absalom and Adonijah, who would later cause trouble in his family. It shows that even famous leaders had complicated families with many children by different women.
entries.3:3: This names the fifth and sixth sons born to David in Hebron, along with their mothers. It completes the count of the six sons he had during that period of his rule.
entries.3:4: This sums up David's time as king: seven and a half years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. It gives the reader a simple timeline of his reign and where his sons were born.
entries.3:5: This lists four more sons born to David in Jerusalem, all by the same mother, Bath-shua. It shows that his family continued to grow after he moved his capital to Jerusalem.
entries.3:6: This begins another group of David's sons born in Jerusalem, naming three of them. These names are part of the official record of his household.
entries.3:7: This adds three more names to the list of David's sons born in Jerusalem. The record keeps track of each child as part of the family line.
entries.3:8: This finishes the Jerusalem list with three more names and notes the total as nine sons. It shows the writer was careful to count and preserve the family record accurately.
entries.3:9: This concludes the list of David's sons, noting he also had sons by servant-wives, and mentions his daughter Tamar. It reminds the reader that David's family included daughters too, and that not every detail of his household is recorded.
entries.3:10: This starts a straight line of kings from Solomon down through Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, and Jehoshaphat. It shows the reader that God kept the royal family line going generation after generation.
entries.3:11: This continues the royal line with Joram, Ahaziah, and Joash. Each name represents a generation of kings descended from David.
entries.3:12: This adds Amaziah, Azariah, and Jotham to the family line of kings. It shows the line kept going without a break through many generations.
entries.3:13: This continues the list with Ahaz, Hezekiah, and Manasseh. It reminds the reader that the royal family included both good and bad kings, yet the line continued.
entries.3:14: This names Amon and then Josiah as the next kings in the line. It brings the family record closer to the time of the nation's later history.
entries.3:15: This lists the sons of Josiah in order, from the oldest to the fourth. It shows how the royal family branched out in the next generation.
entries.3:16: This names the sons of Jehoiakim, including Jeconiah, who would be taken captive. It hints that the family line would continue even through hard times.
entries.3:17: This notes that Jeconiah was taken prisoner and names his son Shealtiel. It shows the reader that God's family line survived even after defeat and exile.
entries.3:18: This lists six more sons of Jeconiah born during or after his captivity. It shows the family kept growing even in difficult circumstances.
entries.3:19: This names the sons of Pedaiah, including Zerubbabel, and lists Zerubbabel's children and their sister. It connects the family line to Zerubbabel, a key figure in the return from exile.
entries.3:20: This adds five more children to Zerubbabel's family. It shows the family line continuing to expand in the generation after the exile.
entries.3:21: This traces the descendants of Hananiah through several generations. It shows the family record being kept carefully long after the return from exile.
entries.3:22: This lists the sons of Shecaniah and then six sons of Shemaiah. It continues the detailed family record into later generations.
entries.3:23: This names the three sons of Neariah. It keeps the family line moving forward one generation at a time.
entries.3:24: This ends the list with the seven sons of Elioenai. It shows the family line of David still existed and was still being recorded many years later.
entries.4:1: This starts a family list for the tribe of Judah, naming Judah's descendants. It reminds the reader that God's story is built through real families and ordinary people.
entries.4:2: This continues the family line from Shobal down to Jahath and his sons, marking a clan called the Zorathites. It shows how one family grew into a whole community.
entries.4:3: These are the children of Hur, including a sister named Hazzelelponi. Listing a sister too shows that women were part of the family record, not forgotten.
entries.4:4: This traces more descendants of Hur, who is linked to the founding of Bethlehem. It quietly connects these old names to a town that later matters greatly in the Bible.
entries.4:5: Ashhur, connected with the town of Tekoa, had two wives named Helah and Naarah. It simply records a family situation as it was.
entries.4:6: Naarah had four sons, and they are named here. Each name preserved is a reminder that these were real people, not just numbers.
entries.4:7: Helah's three sons are listed. The record keeps track of both sides of the family.
entries.4:8: Koz's sons and another family group are named. These short entries show how the tribe spread into many branches.
entries.4:9: Jabez was more respected than his brothers, and his mother named him Jabez because she gave birth to him in pain. His name carried the memory of her suffering.
entries.4:10: Jabez asked God to bless him, enlarge his territory, stay with him, and keep him from harm, and God granted it. It shows that God listens when someone honestly asks him for help and protection.
entries.4:11: This lists Chelub's family line through Mehir to Eshton. It is another small link in the larger family record.
entries.4:12: Eshton's sons and a group called the men of Recah are named. The list keeps showing how the clan spread out.
entries.4:13: Kenaz's sons included Othniel, a well-known leader, and Seraiah. It ties an important figure back to his family roots.
entries.4:14: Seraiah's line leads to Joab, whose descendants were skilled craftsmen. It honors ordinary workers whose skills helped their community.
entries.4:15: Caleb's sons and his grandson Kenaz are listed. This keeps the record of a significant family within Judah.
entries.4:16: Jehallelel's four sons are named. Each entry preserves the memory of a family branch.
entries.4:17: This lists Ezrah's sons and the children of Bithiah, an Egyptian princess married to Mered. It shows that people from outside Israel were welcomed into the family line.
entries.4:18: Mered's wife from Judah had three sons who founded towns. The record shows a family's lasting mark on the land.
entries.4:19: The sons of Hodiah's wife are linked to two towns. It is a brief note connecting families to places.
entries.4:20: Shimon's and Ishi's sons are named. The list keeps a record of even small family groups.
entries.4:21: Shelah's sons are listed, including families known for making fine linen. It shows that people's trades were part of their identity.
entries.4:22: This mentions men who ruled in Moab and later returned to Bethlehem, from very old records. It hints at a history of movement and return that has been carefully preserved.
entries.4:23: These were potters and gardeners who lived in walled settlements and worked for the king. It reminds us that everyday laborers were part of God's people too.
entries.4:24: This begins the family list of Simeon, another son of Jacob. It shifts the record to a different tribe.
entries.4:25: The line continues from Shaul down through Shallum, Mibsam, and Mishma. It traces the family through several generations.
entries.4:26: Mishma's descendants down to Shimei are named. The record keeps following the family line.
entries.4:27: Shimei had many children, but his relatives had few, so Simeon's tribe stayed smaller than Judah's. It honestly notes that not every family grows the same.
entries.4:28: This lists towns where Simeon's people lived, starting with Beersheba. It shows where this tribe actually settled.
entries.4:29: More of their towns are named here. The list maps out the places they called home.
entries.4:30: The towns continue, including Hormah and Ziklag. These places later appear elsewhere in Israel's story.
entries.4:31: The list of towns ends with a note that these were theirs until David became king. It marks a change in how the land was held.
entries.4:32: Five smaller towns of Simeon are named. It shows the tribe lived in many small settlements, not one big city.
entries.4:33: This describes the villages around the towns, reaching to Baalath-beer, and notes that family records were kept. It shows the people cared about remembering where they came from.
entries.4:34: Several family leaders are named here. These were the heads of important households.
entries.4:35: The list continues with more names and family lines. It builds a record of leadership within the tribe.
entries.4:36: More leaders are named in this group. Each name represents a family that mattered to the community.
entries.4:37: Ziza's family line is traced back several generations. It shows careful record-keeping of ancestry.
entries.4:38: These named men were family chiefs, and their families grew very large. It shows how God had blessed them with numbers.
entries.4:39: They went toward Gedor to find pasture for their flocks. It shows them acting practically to care for their animals and families.
entries.4:40: They found rich, peaceful grassland where descendants of Ham had lived before. It describes a good land that had been occupied by others, setting up what comes next.
entries.4:41: During King Hezekiah's reign, these named men attacked the Meunim living in that area, destroyed them, and settled there because the land had good pasture for their flocks. It shows God's people taking possession of land they needed, and reminds us that plans and timing matter in how things unfold.
entries.4:42: Five hundred men from the tribe of Simeon, led by four sons of Ishi, traveled to the hill country of Seir. This is a simple record of a group setting out under clear leaders, showing that organized leadership helped them carry out their mission.
entries.4:43: They killed the remaining Amalekites who had escaped and settled in that land, where their descendants lived from then on. It describes the end of a long conflict and the people making a permanent home in the place they had taken.
entries.5:1: Reuben was Israel's firstborn, but he lost his special firstborn rights because he slept with his father's wife. This shows that being first in line means nothing if you do wrong.
entries.5:2: Judah became the strongest tribe and produced Israel's rulers, but the firstborn rights still went to Joseph's family. God's plans don't always follow the usual order.
entries.5:3: This lists the four sons of Reuben, Israel's oldest son. It's a family record showing who came from Reuben.
entries.5:4: This continues the family line from Joel down through several generations. It's a record of who descended from whom.
entries.5:5: The family line keeps going through Micah, Reaiah, and Baal. These names trace the family's history.
entries.5:6: Beerah was the leader of Reuben's tribe when the Assyrian king took him away as a captive. It's a sad reminder that even leaders can be carried off.
entries.5:7: This lists Reuben's relatives by their family groups, naming Jeiel and Zechariah as leaders. It's a record of the clan's leading men.
entries.5:8: Bela's family line is traced back through several ancestors, and he lived in the area from Aroer to Nebo and Baal-meon. This shows where this family settled.
entries.5:9: Their land stretched east to the edge of the desert near the Euphrates River because their herds had grown so large. God had blessed them with growth, so they needed more room.
entries.5:10: During Saul's reign they defeated the Hagarites and took over the land east of Gilead. This shows God giving them victory in battle.
entries.5:11: The tribe of Gad lived across from Reuben's people, in the land of Bashan up to Salecah. It's a note about where the Gadites settled.
entries.5:12: This names the leaders of Gad: Joel first, Shapham second, then Janai and Shaphat. It records who led this tribe in Bashan.
entries.5:13: This lists seven relatives from Gad's family groups. It's a record of the men who made up their clan.
entries.5:14: These men are traced back through a long family line to Abihail and beyond. It shows their family heritage.
entries.5:15: Ahi was the head of these families, and his line is traced through Abdiel and Guni. It identifies who led this group.
entries.5:16: They lived in Gilead, in Bashan's towns, and across the pasturelands as far as Sirion. This describes the land where they made their home.
entries.5:17: All these family records were made during the reigns of Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam of Israel. It tells us when this census was taken.
entries.5:18: The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh had over forty-four thousand fighting men skilled with shields, swords, and bows. They were a strong and well-trained army.
entries.5:19: They went to war against the Hagarites and three other groups, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. This shows they faced several enemies at once.
entries.5:20: God helped them win because they prayed to him and trusted him during the battle. It reminds us that trusting God in hard times brings his help.
entries.5:21: They captured huge numbers of camels, sheep, donkeys, and people from their enemies. The victory was complete and the spoils were great.
entries.5:22: Many enemies died because God had decided the battle's outcome, and the tribes then lived in that land until they were later taken captive. God's purpose was fulfilled, but their story didn't end there.
entries.5:23: The half-tribe of Manasseh grew in number and spread across the land from Bashan to Mount Hermon. God blessed them with growth and territory.
entries.5:24: This names seven family leaders who were brave warriors and respected men. It honors the leaders of this tribe.
entries.5:25: But they turned away from God and worshiped the gods of the peoples God had driven out. This shows how easy it is to forget God and follow what's around us.
entries.5:26: So God stirred up the Assyrian kings to take these tribes captive to distant lands, where they remained. Turning from God led to losing their homeland.
entries.6:1: This lists the three main family groups descended from Levi, the ancestor of Israel's priests and temple workers. It reminds the reader that God's service was passed down through real families and generations.
entries.6:2: This narrows the family line to Kohath's sons, one of whom was Amram. It shows how the record traces the family branch that would lead to Moses and Aaron.
entries.6:3: Amram's children were Aaron, Moses, and Miriam, and Aaron's sons are named here too. This connects Israel's great leaders and first priests to one ordinary family line.
entries.6:4: The family line continues from Eleazar to his son Phinehas and then Abishua. It shows the priestly line carrying on from one generation to the next.
entries.6:5: The list keeps going with Bukki and then Uzzi. Each name marks another link in the chain of priestly descent.
entries.6:6: Zerahiah and Meraioth are added to the family record. The writer is carefully preserving who came from whom over many years.
entries.6:7: Meraioth's son was Amariah, and his son was Ahitub. This continues the steady record of the priestly family through time.
entries.6:8: Ahitub's son was Zadok, and Zadok's son was Ahimaaz. Zadok became an important priest in Israel's history, and here his place in the family is shown.
entries.6:9: The line moves from Ahimaaz to Azariah and then Johanan. It keeps tracing the priests generation by generation.
entries.6:10: Johanan's son Azariah is noted as the priest who served in the temple Solomon built in Jerusalem. This ties the family record to a specific, well-known place of worship.
entries.6:11: The record continues with Amariah and then Ahitub. It shows the priestly line still active long after earlier generations.
entries.6:12: Ahitub's son was Zadok, and Zadok's son was Shallum. Another Zadok appears here, showing the family name carried on.
entries.6:13: Shallum's son was Hilkiah, and Hilkiah's son was Azariah. The list keeps connecting each priest to his father.
entries.6:14: Azariah's son was Seraiah, and Seraiah's son was Jehozadak. This brings the family line close to the time of exile.
entries.6:15: Jehozadak was taken away as a captive when Nebuchadnezzar conquered Judah and Jerusalem. It shows that even the priestly family shared in the nation's suffering and exile.
entries.6:16: The record returns to Levi's three sons: Gershom, Kohath, and Merari. This restates the starting point before listing the other family branches.
entries.6:17: Gershom's sons are named as Libni and Shimei. It begins to trace the family lines of the other Levite groups.
entries.6:18: Kohath's sons are listed again: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. This repeats the branch that included the priests.
entries.6:19: Merari's sons were Mahli and Mushi, and the writer notes these are the Levite family groups named after their fathers. It organizes the people by their ancestral households.
entries.6:20: This begins a list of Gershom's descendants: Libni, Jahath, and Zimmah. It shows the family line continuing through several generations.
entries.6:21: The Gershom line continues with Joah, Iddo, Zerah, and Jeatherai. Each name represents another generation of Levite families.
entries.6:22: This starts the Kohathite line with Amminadab, Korah, and Assir. It traces a different branch of the same Levite family.
entries.6:23: The line continues with Elkanah, Ebiasaph, and Assir. It shows the family growing and continuing over time.
entries.6:24: Tahath, Uriel, Uzziah, and Shaul are added to the family record. These names preserve the memory of ordinary people in the service of God.
entries.6:25: Elkanah's sons are named as Amasai and Ahimoth. The record keeps following the family forward.
entries.6:26: The line goes through Zophai and Nahath. It is a careful record of who belonged to this family branch.
entries.6:27: Eliab, Jeroham, Elkanah, and Samuel are listed here. This is the same Samuel who became a prophet and leader in Israel.
entries.6:28: Samuel's sons are named as Joel the oldest and Abiah the second. It shows that even a great leader's family had its own next generation.
entries.6:29: This begins the Merari family line with Mahli, Libni, Shimei, and Uzzah. It traces another group of Levites who served in worship.
entries.6:30: The Merari line ends with Shimea, Haggiah, and Asaiah. These names complete this branch of the family record.
entries.6:31: David appointed these men to lead the music in the Lord's house after the ark was finally settled in place. It shows that worship through song was an organized and important part of Israel's life.
entries.6:32: They led worship with songs at the tent of meeting until Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem, and they served in their assigned turns. It shows faithful service continuing through changing times and places.
entries.6:33: Heman led the music, and his family line is traced back through Joel to Samuel. This connects the worship leader to the well-known prophet Samuel.
entries.6:34: The family line continues through Elkanah, Jeroham, Eliel, and Toah. It shows the long heritage behind the man leading worship.
entries.6:35: Zuph, Elkanah, Mahath, and Amasai are listed in the family line. Each name is a link in the chain of Heman's ancestors.
entries.6:36: The line goes through Elkanah, Joel, Azariah, and Zephaniah. It keeps tracing the family back through many generations.
entries.6:37: Tahath, Assir, Ebiasaph, and Korah are named here. This connects Heman's family to the well-known Korah.
entries.6:38: The line goes back through Izhar, Kohath, Levi, and Israel. This shows Heman was a true descendant of Levi and part of God's chosen people.
entries.6:39: Asaph, Heman's brother, stood at his right hand in the music service. It shows the worship team was made up of close family members working together.
entries.6:40: Asaph's family line is traced through Michael, Baaseiah, and Malchijah. It shows that the other worship leader also had a long family heritage.
entries.6:41: The family line continues with the next names in the record. It keeps showing that these worship leaders came from real, remembered families.
entries.6:42: The family line continues with more names of ancestors. Each name matters because it shows this person belonged to a real family with a history of faith.
entries.6:43: The list ends by tracing the line back to Levi, the ancestor of all the temple workers. It shows the reader that this family's role in worship went back a very long way.
entries.6:44: This starts a matching list for the other group of temple workers, the family of Merari, naming their ancestors. It shows that every group of servants had its own place and history.
entries.6:45: More names continue the family line of these temple workers. The reader sees that God's work was carried on by many ordinary families over many years.
entries.6:46: The list keeps going back through the generations. It reminds the reader that faithfulness was passed down from parents to children.
entries.6:47: This line also ends at Merari and then Levi, the ancestor of the temple workers. It shows these people had a clear, God-given place among his servants.
entries.6:48: The rest of the temple workers were given the job of doing all the practical work around the tent where God was worshiped. It shows the reader that behind-the-scenes service for God is real and important work.
entries.6:49: Only Aaron and his descendants were allowed to offer the sacrifices and do the most sacred duties, including dealing with Israel's sin. It shows the reader that God set up a specific way for people to be forgiven and to approach him.
entries.6:50: This begins a list of Aaron's descendants, the priests, from one generation to the next. It shows the reader that the priestly role was handed down in a family line.
entries.6:51: The priestly family line continues with more names. Each generation took its turn serving God in the same sacred role.
entries.6:52: More names carry the priestly line forward. It reminds the reader that God's worship was kept going steadily, generation after generation.
entries.6:53: The list ends with Zadok and Ahimaaz, well-known priests in Israel's history. It shows the reader that this family line produced faithful leaders in worship.
entries.6:54: This begins a list of the towns where these priestly families were to live. The descendants of Aaron got first pick because of their special role. It shows the reader that God made sure his servants had homes and places to live.
entries.6:55: The priests were given Hebron and the land around it in Judah. It shows the reader that God provided specific, real places for the people who served him.
entries.6:56: The open fields around Hebron went to Caleb and his family instead. It shows the reader that God's provision was carefully arranged so different families each got what they needed.
entries.6:57: The priests received Hebron, a city of refuge where someone could flee for safety, along with several other towns. It shows the reader that God cares about both worship and justice and safety for people in trouble.
entries.6:58: More towns are named as belonging to the priests. It shows the reader that God's servants were spread out among the people, not crowded into one place.
entries.6:59: The list of priestly towns continues. Each town gave the priests a place to live and serve among the wider community.
entries.6:60: Three towns from the tribe of Benjamin are added, making thirteen towns in all for the priests. It shows the reader that God kept his promise to provide for those who served him.
entries.6:61: The other families of temple workers received ten towns from several other tribes. It shows the reader that God made sure every group of his servants had a place to live.
entries.6:62: The family of Gershom received thirteen towns from four different tribes. It shows the reader that God's care reached every family that served him.
entries.6:63: The family of Merari received twelve towns from three tribes. It shows the reader that God provided fairly for each group of temple workers.
entries.6:64: The people of Israel gave these towns and their surrounding land to the temple workers. It shows the reader that supporting those who serve God was a shared responsibility of the whole community.
entries.6:65: These towns were assigned from the land of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin. It shows the reader that God's plan for his servants was worked out in real places and real land.
entries.6:66: The families of Kohath received towns from the tribe of Ephraim. It shows the reader that God placed his servants among different tribes so they could serve the whole nation.
entries.6:67: Shechem, another city of refuge, was given to them along with Gezer. It shows the reader that God cared about providing safety for people as well as places for worship.
entries.6:68: Two more towns are named for these temple workers. It shows the reader that God's provision was detailed and specific, not vague.
entries.6:69: The list of towns for the Kohath families ends with two more names. It shows the reader that God made sure his servants had enough places to live and work.
entries.6:70: The rest of the Kohath families received two towns from the half-tribe of Manasseh. It shows the reader that even the smaller groups of God's servants were not forgotten.
entries.6:71: The family of Gershom received two towns from the half-tribe of Manasseh. It shows the reader that God provided for each family group according to its needs.
entries.6:72: Two towns from the tribe of Issachar were given to the Gershom families. It shows the reader that God's servants were spread across the land to serve the people.
entries.6:73: Two more towns are added to their list. It shows the reader that God's care for his servants was steady and complete.
entries.6:74: Two towns from the tribe of Asher were given to them. It shows the reader that God's provision reached into every part of the country.
entries.6:75: Two more towns are named for these temple workers. It shows the reader that God's plan included homes and land for everyone who served him.
entries.6:76: Three towns from the tribe of Naphtali completed their share. It shows the reader that God kept his promise to provide for the families who served at his tent.
entries.6:77: The remaining Merari families received two towns from the tribe of Zebulun. It shows the reader that God made sure even the last group of temple workers had a place to live.
entries.6:78: Four towns east of the Jordan River were given to them from the tribe of Reuben. It shows the reader that God's care extended to his servants on both sides of the river.
entries.6:79: Two more towns are named for these families. It shows the reader that God's provision was complete and carefully recorded.
entries.6:80: Two towns from the tribe of Gad are listed for them. It shows the reader that God provided for his servants all across the land, and every family had a home.
entries.6:81: This verse lists two more towns, Heshbon and Jazer, along with the pastureland around them, that were given to the Levites. It's a reminder that God made sure the people who served in worship had places to live and land to support them.
entries.7:1: This lists the four sons of Issachar, one of Israel's tribes. It reminds the reader that each family line was remembered and recorded.
entries.7:2: Tola's descendants were organized by family and counted as fighting men, numbering over twenty-two thousand in David's time. It shows how large and structured these family groups had become.
entries.7:3: Uzzi's line produced five sons, all described as chiefs. It shows that leadership in these families was passed down through specific people.
entries.7:4: These families had many wives and children, which produced thirty-six thousand fighting men. It reflects how family size and marriage shaped a tribe's strength.
entries.7:5: In total, Issachar's families counted eighty-seven thousand strong fighting men. The writer is showing the tribe's overall size and military strength.
entries.7:6: This begins the record of Benjamin's three sons. It marks a shift to a new tribe in the family list.
entries.7:7: Bela's five sons were family heads and fighting men, numbering over twenty-two thousand. It again ties family leadership to military strength.
entries.7:8: This names the nine sons of Becher. It simply preserves the family line for later generations.
entries.7:9: Becher's descendants were counted as family heads and fighting men, over twenty thousand in all. It shows the size of this branch of Benjamin.
entries.7:10: This lists Jediael's grandson Bilhan and his seven sons. It continues tracing the family line in detail.
entries.7:11: Jediael's descendants totaled seventeen thousand two hundred fighting men fit for war. It shows this family's contribution to the tribe's army.
entries.7:12: This briefly names Shuppim, Huppim, and Dan's son Hushim. It keeps these smaller family lines in the record.
entries.7:13: This lists Naphtali's four sons, noting their mother was Bilhah. It connects the tribe to its family origins.
entries.7:14: This begins Manasseh's line through his servant-wife, naming Machir as Gilead's father. It shows that family lines could run through secondary wives too.
entries.7:15: This notes Gilead's wife Maacah, his sister Hammoleketh, and his brother Zelophehad, who had only daughters. It fills in the family connections around Gilead.
entries.7:16: Maacah bore Peresh and Sheresh, and Sheresh's sons were Ulam and Rakem. It continues the family line through Gilead's household.
entries.7:17: Ulam's son was Bedan, all traced back through Gilead, Machir, and Manasseh. It shows how the writer links each person to the larger tribe.
entries.7:18: Gilead's sister Hammoleketh had three sons. It shows that women in these records could also be named as mothers of family lines.
entries.7:19: This names Shemida's four sons. It adds another branch to the family record.
entries.7:20: This traces Ephraim's line through several generations, with repeated names like Tahath. It shows the family tree continuing over time.
entries.7:21: Ezer and Elead were killed by men of Gath when they tried to take their cattle. It is a sad reminder that these families faced real danger and loss.
entries.7:22: Ephraim mourned his sons for a long time, and his brothers came to comfort him. It shows grief and family support even among these ancient ancestors.
entries.7:23: Ephraim later had another son and named him Beriah because trouble had come to his family. The name itself carried the memory of their sorrow.
entries.7:24: Ephraim's daughter Sheerah built several towns. It shows that women could play a significant role in establishing places.
entries.7:25: This continues Ephraim's line through Rephah, Resheph, Telah, and Tahan. It keeps the family tree moving forward.
entries.7:26: The line continues through Ladan, Ammihud, and Elishama. Each generation is linked to the next.
entries.7:27: The line ends here with Nun and his son Joshua, the famous leader. It shows that Joshua came from this same family line.
entries.7:28: This describes the towns and lands where these families lived, from Bethel to Gezer and Shechem. It grounds the family record in real places.
entries.7:29: Manasseh's descendants lived near towns like Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo, and Dor. It shows the tribes of Joseph settling across a wide area.
entries.7:30: This lists Asher's sons and his daughter Serah. It begins the record of another tribe.
entries.7:31: Beriah's sons were Heber and Malchiel, who was Birzaith's father. It continues Asher's family line.
entries.7:32: Heber's sons are named, along with their sister Shua. It shows sisters were sometimes included in these records.
entries.7:33: This names Japhlet's three sons. It adds another branch to Asher's family tree.
entries.7:34: Shomer's sons are listed here. It keeps track of each family within the tribe.
entries.7:35: Hotham's four sons are named. It continues the detailed family record.
entries.7:36: This begins a longer list of Zophah's sons. It shows how large some of these families became.
entries.7:37: The list of Zophah's sons continues with six more names. It completes that branch of the family.
entries.7:38: Jether's three sons are named. It adds another line to Asher's descendants.
entries.7:39: Ulla's three sons are listed. It finishes this section of the family record.
entries.7:40: All these were Asher's descendants, strong fighting men and leaders, numbering twenty-six thousand in the army. It summarizes the tribe's strength and closes the record.
entries.8:1: This starts a family list for the tribe of Benjamin, naming Bela as the firstborn and his brothers in order. It reminds the reader that God kept track of ordinary families through generations.
entries.8:2: The list of Benjamin's sons continues with Nohah and Rapha. Each name shows that real people, not just numbers, made up this family line.
entries.8:3: Here the record moves to Bela's own sons, including Gera, who was the father of Ehud. It shows how one generation leads into the next in this family.
entries.8:4: More of Bela's sons are named: Abishua, Naaman, and Ahoah. The writer is carefully preserving the family's memory.
entries.8:5: The last of Bela's sons listed are Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram. These names may seem unimportant, but they show that every person in the family was counted.
entries.8:6: This lists the sons of Ehud, who were leaders of family groups living in Geba. It shows that some of these families settled in a particular town.
entries.8:7: Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera are named, and Gera's sons Uzza and Ahihud are mentioned. The record keeps following the family branches.
entries.8:8: Shaharaim had children in Moab after he sent away his wives Hushim and Beerah. This is a brief note about a complicated family situation in a foreign land.
entries.8:9: With his wife Hodesh, Shaharaim had sons named Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, and Malcam. The list continues to show how his family grew.
entries.8:10: Jeuz, Shachia, and Mirmah are named as Shaharaim's sons, and they became heads of family groups. This means they were leaders within their extended families.
entries.8:11: Hushim, one of Shaharaim's earlier wives, had sons named Abitub and Elpaal. The record keeps track of each branch of the family.
entries.8:12: Elpaal's sons included Eber, Misham, and Shemed, who built the towns of Ono and Lod and their surrounding villages. This shows that some in this family were builders and settlers.
entries.8:13: Beriah and Shema were family leaders in Aijalon who drove out the people of Gath. This tells the reader that these men were known for a military victory.
entries.8:14: Shashak and Jeremoth are named as brothers of the previous men. The family record continues with another branch.
entries.8:15: Zebadiah, Arad, and Eder are listed next. These are more names in the growing family tree.
entries.8:16: Michael, Ishpah, and Joha are identified as sons of Beriah. The writer is showing which father each man belonged to.
entries.8:17: Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, and Heber are named here. The list keeps moving through the family's generations.
entries.8:18: Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab are named as sons of Elpaal. This connects them to the earlier mention of Elpaal's line.
entries.8:19: Jakim, Zichri, and Zabdi appear next in the record. Each name adds to the picture of this tribe's families.
entries.8:20: Elienai, Zillethai, and Eliel are listed. The writer is carefully working through the family groups.
entries.8:21: Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath are named as sons of Shimei. This shows another branch of the family.
entries.8:22: Ishpan, Eber, and Eliel are listed next. The record continues without comment, just preserving the names.
entries.8:23: Abdon, Zichri, and Hanan are named here. These are more members of the tribe of Benjamin.
entries.8:24: Hananiah, Elam, and Anathothijah appear in the list. The writer is making sure none of these family members are forgotten.
entries.8:25: Iphdeiah and Penuel are named as sons of Shashak. This ties them back to an earlier family leader.
entries.8:26: Shamsherai, Shehariah, and Athaliah are listed. The family record keeps growing with each verse.
entries.8:27: Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri are named as sons of Jeremoth. This closes out one section of the family list.
entries.8:28: These men were heads of families and chief men, and they lived in Jerusalem. This tells the reader that some of Benjamin's descendants settled in the important city of Jerusalem.
entries.8:29: Jeiel, called the father of Gibeon, lived in Gibeon, and his wife was Maacah. This introduces a new family line connected to another town.
entries.8:30: Jeiel's oldest son was Abdon, followed by Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, and Nadab. The list shows the order of sons in this family.
entries.8:31: Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth are named next. These are more sons in Jeiel's family line.
entries.8:32: Mikloth's son was Shimeah, and these families lived in Jerusalem alongside their relatives. This shows family groups settling near each other.
entries.8:33: Ner was the father of Abner, and Kish was the father of Saul, Israel's first king, whose sons included Jonathan and Eshbaal. This connects the family list to well-known figures in Israel's history.
entries.8:34: Jonathan's son was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal's son was Micah. This continues the royal family line after Saul and Jonathan.
entries.8:35: Micah's sons were Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz. The record keeps following the descendants of Saul's family.
entries.8:36: Ahaz was the father of Jehoaddah, whose sons included Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri, and Zimri was the father of Moza. This shows the family line continuing through several generations.
entries.8:37: Moza was the father of Binea, and the line continued through Raphah, Eleasah, and Azel. Each generation is named in order.
entries.8:38: Azel had five sons: Azrikam the oldest, then Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. This completes the record of Azel's immediate family.
entries.8:39: Eshek, Azel's brother, had sons named Ulam, Jeush, and Eliphelet. This adds a side branch to the family tree.
entries.8:40: Ulam's sons were warriors who used bows, and his family grew to a hundred and fifty descendants. The chapter ends by saying all these were sons of Benjamin, tying the whole list back to one ancestor.
entries.9:1: This verse sums up that all Israel's families were recorded in official royal records, and it notes that Judah was carried off to Babylon as punishment for their sin. It reminds the reader that God keeps account of His people and that sin has real consequences.
entries.9:2: After the exile, the first people to resettle their family lands were ordinary Israelites along with the priests, Levites, and temple servants. It shows that restoring worship and community life was the priority for those returning home.
entries.9:3: Some people from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh settled in Jerusalem. It shows that people from different tribes came together to rebuild life in the holy city.
entries.9:4: This lists Uthai's family line back to Perez, son of Judah. It shows that even ordinary residents of Jerusalem had a clear, remembered heritage.
entries.9:5: This names Asaiah, the oldest of the Shilonite clan, and his sons. It simply records which family group lived in Jerusalem.
entries.9:6: This counts 690 men from the Zerah clan living in Jerusalem. It shows the city was repopulated by specific, numbered families.
entries.9:7: This begins listing the men from the tribe of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem, starting with Sallu. It shows Benjamin's families were part of rebuilding the city.
entries.9:8: This continues naming Benjaminite men and their family lines. It shows the careful record-keeping of who lived where after the return.
entries.9:9: These men's relatives totaled 956, all heads of families listed by their fathers' names. It shows the community was organized by family and that leaders were clearly identified.
entries.9:10: This lists the priests living in Jerusalem: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, and Jachin. It shows that priestly families were settled in the city to serve at the temple.
entries.9:11: This traces Azariah's line back to Zadok and Ahitub and notes he was the ruler of the house of God. It shows a qualified leader was put in charge of temple affairs.
entries.9:12: This names more priests and their family lines. It shows the priestly work was shared among several established families.
entries.9:13: These priests' relatives totaled 1,760 capable men who did the work of God's house. It shows a large, organized group was dedicated to temple service.
entries.9:14: This begins listing the Levites living in Jerusalem, starting with Shemaiah from the Merari clan. It shows the Levites were also settled and organized for service.
entries.9:15: This names more Levites, including Mattaniah from the family of Asaph. It shows the temple staff included people from well-known worship families.
entries.9:16: This names Obadiah and Berechiah, whose families lived in the villages of the Netophathites. It shows even Levites in outlying towns were part of the temple workforce.
entries.9:17: This lists the gatekeepers, with Shallum as their chief. It shows that guarding the entrances was an organized, important job.
entries.9:18: These gatekeepers had served at the king's gate on the east side and had guarded the entrances of the Levites' tents. It shows their role had a long history of protecting holy places.
entries.9:19: Shallum and his Korahite relatives were responsible for the worship order and guarding the tent's doors, as their ancestors had done. It shows faithfulness in service was passed down through generations.
entries.9:20: In earlier times Phinehas son of Eleazar had been their leader, and the writer adds a blessing asking the Lord to be with him. It shows respect for godly leadership from the past.
entries.9:21: Zechariah son of Meshelemiah was the gatekeeper at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. It shows a specific person was assigned to guard the place of worship.
entries.9:22: There were 212 gatekeepers, listed by family, whom David and Samuel had appointed to their posts. It shows that orderly, trustworthy appointments were made for temple service.
entries.9:23: These men and their sons guarded the doors of the Lord's house, the tent, as watchmen. It shows guarding God's house was a serious, ongoing family responsibility.
entries.9:24: The gatekeepers stood guard on all four sides—east, west, north, and south. It shows the house of God was carefully protected from every direction.
entries.9:25: Their relatives in nearby villages came in every seven days to join them on duty. It shows the gatekeeping work was shared on a rotating schedule.
entries.9:26: The four chief gatekeepers, who were Levites, had the special job of overseeing the rooms and storehouses of God's house. It shows trusted leaders handled the temple's resources.
entries.9:27: They slept around the house of God because they were responsible for guarding it and opening it each morning. It shows their devotion involved being present day and night.
entries.9:28: Some of them were in charge of the worship utensils, keeping count of what went in and came out. It shows careful accountability was part of serving God.
entries.9:29: Others were responsible for the holy items and supplies like flour, wine, oil, incense, and spices. It shows even practical supplies for worship were handled by assigned people.
entries.9:30: Some of the priests' sons were responsible for mixing the spices. It shows specific tasks in worship were given to specific people.
entries.9:31: Mattithiah, a Levite and oldest son of Shallum the Korahite, was in charge of baking the flat cakes. It shows humble, practical work was part of temple service.
entries.9:32: Some Kohathite Levites were responsible for preparing the holy bread and setting it out before the Lord every Sabbath. It shows regular, faithful preparation was needed for worship.
entries.9:33: These Levite family heads led the music and singing, living in the temple rooms and free from other work because their duty continued day and night. It shows worship through music was a full-time, devoted calling.
entries.9:34: These were the chief Levite family heads, and they lived in Jerusalem. It shows the leaders of worship and service were settled in the city.
entries.9:35: Jeiel, the father of Gibeon, lived in Gibeon, and his wife was named Maacah. It introduces a family line connected to Saul's ancestry.
entries.9:36: This lists Jeiel's sons, beginning with Abdon his oldest, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, and Nadab. It records the family line leading toward Saul.
entries.9:37: This continues the list with Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth. It simply records more members of this family line.
entries.9:38: Mikloth was the father of Shimeam, and these families lived in Jerusalem alongside their relatives. It shows family groups were settled close together.
entries.9:39: This traces the line from Ner to Kish to Saul, and names Saul's sons Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal. It connects the record to Israel's first king and his family.
entries.9:40: Jonathan's son was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal was the father of Micah. It continues Saul's family line, showing the record was kept even after the monarchy ended.
entries.9:41: This lists the sons of a man named Micah, continuing a family record. It reminds the reader that ordinary families and their names mattered to God and were remembered.
entries.9:42: This traces the family line from Ahaz down through Jarah to Zimri and Moza. It shows that each generation passed the family story on, and that God keeps track of ordinary people across time.
entries.9:43: The family line continues from Moza to Binea and then down to Azel. It is a simple record of generations, showing that faithfulness carries on quietly from parent to child.
entries.9:44: Azel had five sons, and all their names are recorded here. The list ends with this family, reminding the reader that every person in a family line is known and valued, not just the famous ones.
entries.10:1: The Philistines attacked Israel, and the Israelite soldiers ran away and were wounded or killed on Mount Gilboa. It shows how a battle can turn into a crushing defeat for God's people.
entries.10:2: The Philistines chased Saul and his sons and killed three of his sons in battle. It means Saul's family lost its heirs in a single day of fighting.
entries.10:3: The fighting closed in on Saul, and enemy archers hit him with arrows and wounded him badly. It shows Saul trapped and hurting with no way to escape.
entries.10:4: Saul asked his armor-bearer to kill him so the Philistines would not torture and mock him, but the man was too afraid, so Saul fell on his own sword. It shows Saul choosing death over capture and disgrace.
entries.10:5: When the armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he killed himself the same way. It shows how deeply loyal and shaken he was by his king's death.
entries.10:6: Saul and his three sons all died, and his royal family line came to an end. It shows the whole house of Saul falling together in one day.
entries.10:7: When the Israelites in the nearby valley saw their army run and their king dead, they abandoned their towns and fled, and the Philistines moved in. It shows how one defeat spread fear and cost people their homes.
entries.10:8: The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found Saul and his sons lying dead on Mount Gilboa. It shows the enemy finding the king's body among the fallen.
entries.10:9: The Philistines stripped Saul's armor, cut off his head, and sent messengers around their land to announce the news to their gods and their people. It shows them treating Israel's king as a trophy of their victory.
entries.10:10: They placed Saul's armor in the temple of their gods and hung his head in the temple of Dagon. It shows them crediting their gods with the win and publicly shaming Saul.
entries.10:11: When the people of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, they responded. It shows that some Israelites still cared about honoring their king.
entries.10:12: Their fighting men traveled to retrieve the bodies of Saul and his sons, buried their bones under a tree in Jabesh, and fasted for seven days. It shows them giving the king an honorable burial and mourning his death.
entries.10:13: Saul died because he sinned against the Lord by disobeying his word and by consulting a medium instead of seeking God. It shows that rejecting God's guidance has serious consequences.
entries.10:14: Saul did not ask the Lord for direction, so God ended his life and gave the kingdom to David, Jesse's son. It shows that God removed Saul and raised up David as king in his place.
entries.11:1: The tribes of Israel came to David and publicly declared that they were his own people, sharing the same family and nation. It means the reader should see that unity and shared identity matter when people come together to follow a leader.
entries.11:2: The people remind David that he already led Israel's army in battle, and God had chosen him to shepherd and rule the nation. It means God's calling on a leader shows up in faithful service before the title ever arrives.
entries.11:3: Israel's leaders make a formal agreement with David at Hebron and anoint him king, just as God had told Samuel. It shows that God keeps his promises, even when the fulfillment takes years.
entries.11:4: David and the whole army march on Jerusalem, which was held by the Jebusites. It marks the moment God's chosen king begins to take the city that will become Israel's capital.
entries.11:5: The Jebusites boast that David cannot get in, but he captures their fortress anyway. It reminds the reader that human confidence against God's purposes does not hold up.
entries.11:6: David promises the top command to whoever leads the attack, and Joab takes the challenge and wins. It shows that courage and initiative were rewarded in David's kingdom.
entries.11:7: David moves into the captured fortress, and it becomes known as the City of David. It is a simple record of how the king made the conquered stronghold his home.
entries.11:8: David rebuilds the city from one end to the other, and Joab repairs the rest. It shows that taking ground is only the start; the work of building and restoring comes next.
entries.11:9: David keeps growing stronger because the Lord of hosts is with him. It teaches that real strength comes from God's presence, not from the person's own ability.
entries.11:10: This begins a list of David's top warriors who backed him and helped make him king over all Israel, as God had promised. It shows that God's plans often move forward through loyal, ordinary people.
entries.11:11: The first warrior listed is Jashobeam, who killed three hundred men with his spear in one battle. It highlights the extraordinary courage of the men who fought for David.
entries.11:12: Eleazar is named next as one of the three mightiest fighters. He stands out among David's elite soldiers for his bravery.
entries.11:13: Eleazar stood with David at Pas-dammim when the Philistines gathered for battle and the Israelite troops fled. It shows that courage often means staying when everyone else runs.
entries.11:14: Eleazar stood his ground in the middle of a barley field, beat back the Philistines, and the Lord gave a great victory. It shows that God can win through one person who refuses to give up.
entries.11:15: Three of David's top warriors came down to him at the cave of Adullam while the Philistine army camped nearby. It shows the loyalty these men had toward their leader in dangerous times.
entries.11:16: David was hiding in the stronghold while a Philistine unit occupied Bethlehem, his hometown. It sets the scene for a moment of longing that leads to a brave act.
entries.11:17: David wistfully wishes someone would bring him a drink from the well by Bethlehem's gate. It shows a very human moment of homesickness in the middle of war.
entries.11:18: The three warriors broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the Bethlehem well, and brought it to David, but he poured it out to the Lord instead of drinking it. It shows that he treated their sacrifice as too precious for his own pleasure.
entries.11:19: David says he could never drink what amounted to the lifeblood of men who risked their lives for him, so he offered it to God. It teaches deep respect for the cost others pay on our behalf.
entries.11:20: Abishai, Joab's brother, was the leader of the thirty and had killed three hundred men with his spear, though he was not counted among the top three. It shows that great achievement does not always bring the highest honor.
entries.11:21: Abishai was the most honored of the thirty and became their captain, but he still did not match the first three. It shows that rank and honor come in different levels among brave men.
entries.11:22: Benaiah from Kabzeel killed two lion-like warriors from Moab and also went down into a pit and killed a lion on a snowy day. It shows remarkable bravery in situations most people would avoid.
entries.11:23: Benaiah also killed a huge Egyptian warrior by snatching the man's own spear and using it against him. It shows quick thinking and courage when the odds were against him.
entries.11:24: These deeds made Benaiah famous among the thirty mighty men. It shows that consistent bravery builds a lasting reputation.
entries.11:25: Benaiah was honored above the thirty but was not equal to the first three, and David put him in charge of his guard. It shows that a trustworthy fighter was given a place of special responsibility.
entries.11:26: This starts the longer list of David's mighty warriors, beginning with Asahel and Elhanan. It shows that David's success rested on many capable men, not just a few famous ones.
entries.11:27: The list continues with Shammoth and Helez, two of David's fighting men. Each name records a real person who served the king faithfully.
entries.11:28: Ira and Abiezer are named among David's warriors. It shows that even lesser-known soldiers were remembered for their part in the kingdom.
entries.11:29: Sibbecai and Ilai are added to the list of David's mighty men. The record honors their service one name at a time.
entries.11:30: Maharai and Heled are listed next. It shows that the king's strength came from many loyal fighters, each one counted.
entries.11:31: Ithai from Benjamin and Benaiah from Pirathon are named. It shows that David's warriors came from different tribes and towns across Israel.
entries.11:32: Hurai and Abiel are included among the mighty men. Their names are preserved as a record of faithful service.
entries.11:33: Azmaveth and Eliahba are listed next. It reminds the reader that every one of these men played a role in David's success.
entries.11:34: The sons of Hashem and Jonathan son of Shage are named. The list keeps honoring the many fighters who stood with David.
entries.11:35: Ahiam and Eliphal are added to the record. It shows that the kingdom was built by a large company of brave men, not a handful.
entries.11:36: Hepher and Ahijah are named among the warriors. Each entry is a small memorial to someone who served the king.
entries.11:37: Hezro and Naarai are listed next. It shows that faithfulness in battle was remembered and recorded.
entries.11:38: Joel and Mibhar are included in the list. The record keeps track of the men who made up David's fighting force.
entries.11:39: Zelek the Ammonite and Naharai, Joab's armor-bearer, are named. It shows that even a foreigner and a servant were counted among David's mighty men.
entries.11:40: Ira and Gareb the Ithrites close out this part of the list. It shows that the record of David's loyal warriors continues to the very end.
entries.11:41: This is a list of David's mighty warriors, including Uriah the Hittite, a foreigner who served him faithfully. It reminds readers that God values loyalty and courage in ordinary people, even outsiders.
entries.11:42: Adina was a leader from the tribe of Reuben who brought thirty men with him to support David. It shows that good leadership means bringing others along to serve a worthy cause.
entries.11:43: Hanan and Joshaphat are named among David's fighting men. Each name matters, showing that God remembers the contributions of people we might otherwise overlook.
entries.11:44: Uzzia, Shama, and Jeiel were among David's warriors, coming from different towns. Their inclusion shows that people from many places joined together to support God's chosen king.
entries.11:45: Jediael and his brother Joha are listed as part of David's fighting force. It reminds us that family members can serve side by side and that faithfulness is worth recording.
entries.11:46: This verse names several more warriors, including Ithmah from Moab, a nation often at odds with Israel. It shows that commitment to David, and to God's purposes, mattered more than a person's background.
entries.11:47: The list ends with Eliel, Obed, and Jaasiel, closing out the roll of David's mighty men. It reminds readers that every person who serves faithfully plays a part, even if their name is only briefly mentioned.
entries.12:1: These were skilled fighting men who came to join David at Ziklag while Saul was still hunting him. It shows that even in hard, dangerous times, people were willing to stand with David and help him.
entries.12:2: These men were experts with bows and could shoot or sling stones with either hand, and they came from Saul's own tribe of Benjamin. Their skill and their choice to back David made them especially valuable.
entries.12:3: This verse simply lists the names of the leaders and men in that group. It reminds us that each person who helped David is remembered by name.
entries.12:4: Ishmaiah was a notable warrior among David's elite fighters and led them, along with several other named men. Even the leaders were willing to serve alongside others.
entries.12:5: This is another short list of men who joined David. The record of their names shows that ordinary individuals mattered in building his support.
entries.12:6: These men came from the Korahite family line. Their inclusion shows that support for David came from many different family groups.
entries.12:7: Two more men from Gedor are named here. The list keeps growing, showing steady, broad support for David.
entries.12:8: Some tough, experienced soldiers from the tribe of Gad left their homes to join David in the wilderness. They were fierce and fast, the kind of loyal fighters any leader would want.
entries.12:9: This begins a list of the Gadite leaders in order of rank. It shows their group was well organized under clear leadership.
entries.12:10: The list of Gadite commanders continues with the fourth and fifth men. Each leader had his place in the order.
entries.12:11: The sixth and seventh commanders are named here. The orderly record shows how these fighting men were structured.
entries.12:12: The eighth and ninth commanders are listed. The count keeps going, showing a full and organized force.
entries.12:13: The tenth and eleventh commanders complete the list. Every leader is named, showing none were forgotten.
entries.12:14: These Gadite leaders were officers over large groups, from a hundred up to a thousand men. Even the least important among them carried real responsibility.
entries.12:15: These men crossed the flooded Jordan River in the spring and drove off the people living in the valleys on both sides. Their courage in a dangerous crossing showed how capable they were.
entries.12:16: Some men from Benjamin and Judah also came to David at his hideout. Support for David was coming from several tribes, not just one.
entries.12:17: David met them and spoke honestly: if they came as friends, he would welcome them, but if they came to betray him, he trusted God to judge them. He was open but also careful, and he left justice in God's hands.
entries.12:18: God's Spirit came on Amasai, who declared that they were truly on David's side and that God was with him. David accepted their pledge and made them officers in his army.
entries.12:19: Some men of Manasseh came to David when he was with the Philistines, but the Philistine leaders distrusted him and sent him away, fearing he would turn back to Saul. Even when others doubted him, God was quietly protecting David.
entries.12:20: When David returned to Ziklag, several Manassite commanders came over to his side. These were men of high rank, and their support strengthened him.
entries.12:21: These men helped David against raiding bands because they were strong warriors and army officers. Their help came at a time when David needed it.
entries.12:22: More and more people joined David every day until his army was huge, like an army sent by God. Steady, growing support showed that God was behind David's rise.
entries.12:23: This begins a count of the armed men who came to Hebron to make David king, just as the Lord had promised. It shows God's plan being carried out by real people.
entries.12:24: Judah sent almost seven thousand armed spearmen. The tribe closest to David gave strong military support.
entries.12:25: Simeon sent over seven thousand experienced fighting men. Their numbers added real strength to David's cause.
entries.12:26: The tribe of Levi sent four thousand six hundred men. Even the priestly tribe took part in supporting David as king.
entries.12:27: Jehoiada, a leader from Aaron's family, came with three thousand seven hundred men. The religious leadership stood behind David too.
entries.12:28: Zadok, a young but capable warrior, came with twenty-two captains from his family. Young men with ability were also part of David's support.
entries.12:29: Benjamin, Saul's own tribe, sent three thousand men, though most of that tribe had stayed loyal to Saul until then. Support for David was growing even among his rival's relatives.
entries.12:30: Ephraim sent over twenty thousand famous fighting men. Large, well-known families threw their weight behind David.
entries.12:31: The half-tribe of Manasseh sent eighteen thousand men, each listed by name, to make David king. Their coming was deliberate and personal, not just a crowd.
